people.name: Gilbert de la O
body: In the early years of the Vietnam War, a young soldier from St. Paul was wounded during Operation Abilene and came home with a Purple Heart. Gilbert de la O spent the next half-century at home, on St. Paul's West Side, where people came to call him the "Godfather of the West Side."

His parents were among the earliest Mexican Americans to settle the river flats, the low land along the Mississippi across from downtown. He was born in St. Paul and graduated from Humboldt High School. The Ramsey County Historical Society records that most of the West Side Flats were cleared in the mid-1960s, so the neighborhood he grew up in had to be rebuilt elsewhere.

De la O helped do that rebuilding. As a teenager he started going to Neighborhood House, the West Side's long-running settlement house. He was later hired there, eventually became its executive director, and was inducted into its Hall of Fame. He helped found the West Side Boosters and was the first Latino to serve on the St. Paul School Board.

In his last years he was fighting cancer. Carlos Mariani, a state representative at the time, said of him: "He insisted on making sure that regular, everyday people were part of problem-solving for communities." De la O died in August 2022 at age 77. In place of flowers, he asked people to spend time with family and friends enjoying a meal around the table.
keyFacts: Born in St. Paul; parents among the earliest Mexican American settlers of the river flats.
Vietnam veteran, wounded in Operation Abilene; Purple Heart.
Neighborhood House from his teens through executive director; Hall of Fame.
Helped found the West Side Boosters.
First Latino member of the St. Paul School Board.
A St. Paul community leader for more than 50 years.

people.name: Martha Castañon
body: When Martha Castañon was 12, in 1972, her father had to register her to work. She keeps that framed certificate and calls it "my degree of hard work." By then she had already worked onion fields in Texas, cucumber fields in Wisconsin and sugar-beet fields in Minnesota. She first worked in the fields at age 10, near Barnesville in the Red River Valley.

Her family first came north when her grandfather left Mexico to help fill a farm-labor shortage during World War II. The Forum of Fargo-Moorhead tells her story against the long history of workers who came north each spring to thin and weed sugar beets along the Minnesota–North Dakota border.

Castañon spent 35 years at Southern Minnesota Regional Legal Services, helping farmworkers and low-income residents with legal problems. She worked there as a secretary for 17 years before being trained and hired as a paralegal, and there she found her passion for immigration work. In 2015 she joined the Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota in Moorhead.

In 2012 she was honored by the Labor Hall of Fame as an advocate for farmworkers, and in 2016 Legal Services of Northwest Minnesota gave her its Partner in Justice Award. On December 9, 2024, the City of Moorhead gave her a Human Rights Award. At that time she was an accredited representative at the Immigrant Law Center and served on the board of the Minnesota Council on Latino Affairs. Accepting the award, she shared her mother's saying, "No te cuesta nada tratar a una persona bien," which she translated as "It costs you nothing to treat a person right."
keyFacts: First worked in the fields at age 10; registered for farm work at 12, in 1972.
35 years at Southern Minnesota Regional Legal Services, from secretary to paralegal.
Joined the Immigrant Law Center of Minnesota in Moorhead in 2015.

people.name: Xavier Tavera
body: In an exhibition that opened September 23, 2017, at the Minnesota History Center, older men from St. Paul's West Side looked out from large portraits. They were Mexican and Mexican American veterans of World War II, Korea and Vietnam, members of AMVETS Post #5, and photographer Xavier Tavera had spent time getting to know each of them. By the University of Minnesota Alumni Association's account, many had enlisted partly as a path to citizenship, and some came home to find their rights as citizens undercut.

Tavera was born in Mexico City in 1971 and took his first photograph there at 13. In 1996 he came to the United States to work as an industrial photographer for a Houston company that later moved its headquarters to St. Paul, and he enrolled at the Minneapolis College of Art and Design. His work focuses on immigrants and on communities that are often unseen. His Borderlands project shows life along the U.S.–Mexico border, including deported veterans.

He was one of four McKnight Fellows in the 2003–04 photography fellows exhibition and has received Minnesota State Arts Board grants. He has taught photography at Augsburg and the University of Minnesota. As of October 2026, Carleton College lists him as an assistant professor of art. He has said that in Mexico he was "nothing," but in Minnesota he is "Mexican and an immigrant and a person of color," a shift that shapes how he sees the people he photographs.
keyFacts: Born in Mexico City in 1971; came to Minnesota in 1996.
McKnight fellowship in photography (2003–04); Minnesota State Arts Board grants.
AMVETS Post #5, Minnesota History Center, September 23, 2017, to April 22, 2018: 35 portraits.
Assistant professor of art, Carleton College, as of October 2026.

people.name: Gustavo Romero
body: In 2020, with restaurants hit by the pandemic, chef Gustavo Romero lost his job at Mercy Bar & Dining Room. He and his wife, Kate, started making tortillas the traditional way: cooking heirloom corn in an alkaline solution, a process called nixtamalization, and grinding it into fresh masa. That was the start of Nixta, a small tortillería in Northeast Minneapolis.

Romero grew up in Tulancingo de Bravo, a couple of hours northeast of Mexico City, and left home at 13. In Tijuana he worked in nightclubs, first as a DJ and then as a server. As a teenager he crossed into San Diego and stayed. He worked in restaurants in Arizona, Oregon and Georgia as a dishwasher, line cook, pastry chef, banquet chef and sous chef. With help from his mentor, Mario Maggi, he spent almost a year in Mexico getting his immigration status legalized. He then trained in Italian cooking in Florence and in classical technique at Le Cordon Bleu, and he led kitchens in San Francisco, Miami and Chicago before he and Kate moved to Minneapolis in 2018.

Nixta buys heirloom corn from family farms in Mexico. In 2023 the Romeros opened Oro by Nixta, a sit-down restaurant next door, earlier than they had planned, after the neighboring space was vacated. In 2024 it was one of ten finalists nationwide for the James Beard Award for Best New Restaurant.
keyFacts: Grew up in Tulancingo de Bravo; left home at 13.
Trained in Florence and at Le Cordon Bleu; moved to Minneapolis in 2018.
Started Nixta after losing his chef job during the pandemic.
2023: Oro by Nixta; 2024: James Beard finalist, Best New Restaurant.

people.name: Jovita Idar
body: In 1911, in Laredo, Texas, a young teacher and journalist helped bring Mexican American communities together to talk about unequal schools and unfair treatment. That October, Jovita Idar became the first president of the Liga Femenil Mexicanista, the League of Mexican Women, which offered free education to Mexican children.

Idar was born September 7, 1885, in Laredo. Her father, Nicasio Idar, was a civil rights advocate who edited the Spanish-language newspaper La Crónica. She earned a teaching certificate in 1903 but left teaching because Mexican American students were segregated and taught in poor conditions. In 1911 La Crónica helped organize the First Mexican Congress, which addressed inequality, education and economic opportunity.

During the Mexican Revolution, Idar crossed the border to nurse the wounded and joined La Cruz Blanca, a relief group similar to the Red Cross. Later, writing for El Progreso, she criticized President Woodrow Wilson's decision to send U.S. troops to the border. A famous story, told by her brother and niece in 1980s interviews, says she stood in the doorway to block Texas Rangers who came to shut the paper down. The Handbook of Texas reports that later research has challenged that account.

After her father died in 1914, she ran La Crónica. In 1917, after marrying Bartolo Juárez, she moved to San Antonio, where she started a free kindergarten, worked as an interpreter for Spanish-speaking hospital patients, edited the Methodist publication El Heraldo Cristiano and was active in the Texas Democratic Party. She died at her home in San Antonio on June 13, 1946. On August 14, 2023, the U.S. Mint put a quarter honoring her into circulation.
keyFacts: 1903: teaching certificate; left teaching over segregation and poor conditions.
1911: helped with the First Mexican Congress; first president of the Liga Femenil Mexicanista.
Nursed the wounded during the Mexican Revolution with La Cruz Blanca.
1917: moved to San Antonio; founded a free kindergarten and interpreted for hospital patients.
2023: honored on a U.S. quarter.

people.name: Héctor P. García
people.field: Medicine, civil rights and veterans' rights
body: In 1949, a funeral director in Texas would not let the family of Private Felix Longoria, a Mexican American soldier killed in World War II, hold services in the funeral home's chapel. A Corpus Christi doctor named Héctor P. García made the case public. Senator Lyndon B. Johnson helped arrange for Longoria to be buried at Arlington National Cemetery, and the case drew national attention to the discrimination Mexican American veterans faced.

García was born January 17, 1914, in Llera, Tamaulipas, Mexico, and moved with his family to Texas in 1918. He graduated as his high school's valedictorian and finished at the University of Texas in 1936. At UT's medical school in Galveston, a quota system left him the only Latino in his class. In 1942 he volunteered for the U.S. Army. He served in Europe and North Africa and received the Bronze Star.

After settling in Corpus Christi, García saw Mexican American veterans being denied the benefits they had earned. In 1948 he founded the American G.I. Forum to fight for them. The group also took on school segregation, the Texas poll tax and discrimination on Texas juries. He organized "Viva Kennedy" clubs in 1960. As an alternate U.S. delegate to the United Nations, on October 26, 1967, he addressed the General Assembly in Spanish, which a 2010 resolution of Congress describes as the first speech there by an American in a language other than English. On March 26, 1984, President Ronald Reagan presented him with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and that resolution calls him the first Mexican American to receive it. He died in Corpus Christi on July 26, 1996.
keyFacts: Born in Llera, Tamaulipas; family moved to Texas in 1918.
World War II Army service in Europe and North Africa; Bronze Star.
1948: founded the American G.I. Forum.
1949: made the Felix Longoria case public.
1967: addressed the UN General Assembly in Spanish.
1984: Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: José M. Hernández
body: On August 28, 2009, Space Shuttle Discovery lifted off for a 14-day mission to the International Space Station. Its flight engineer had grown up in a family that worked California's fields. By Arte Público Press's account, José M. Hernández was the first migrant farmworker to become a NASA astronaut.

Hernández was born on August 7, 1962, in French Camp, California, into a migrant farmworking family from Mexico; he considers nearby Stockton his hometown. The family followed the "California circuit." Each March they traveled from Mexico to California's southern San Joaquin Valley, worked their way north to the Stockton area by summer, and returned to Mexico in late November. Moving so often meant changing schools all the time, and he did not learn English until he was 12. He went on to earn undergraduate and graduate degrees in electrical engineering.

At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, he worked on an X-ray laser, helped develop the first full-field digital mammography system and worked on nuclear non-proliferation. NASA selected him in 2004, and he flew as flight engineer on STS-128. He told his story in the memoir Reaching for the Stars (2012), which became the basis for the film A Million Miles Away.
keyFacts: Born in French Camp, California; did not learn English until age 12.
Lawrence Livermore: helped develop the first full-field digital mammography system.
2004: selected by NASA.
2009: flight engineer on STS-128.
2012: memoir Reaching for the Stars.

people.name: Sandra Cisneros
body: A girl named Esperanza longs for a house of her own, away from a crowded Chicago street. Sandra Cisneros published The House on Mango Street in 1984. By the National Women's History Museum's account, the novel has sold more than six million copies.

Cisneros was born December 20, 1954, in Chicago. Both of her parents were from Mexico, and she was the only daughter among seven children. She earned a bachelor's degree in English from Loyola University of Chicago in 1976 and an MFA in creative writing from the University of Iowa in 1978. Her first book was the poetry collection Bad Boys (1980).

The House on Mango Street won the American Book Award the following year. Her story collection Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories (1991) won the PEN Center West Award for Best Fiction. She received fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts and, in 1995, the MacArthur Foundation. She founded the Macondo Foundation to support writers, and in 2016 President Barack Obama presented her with the National Medal of Arts. An opera of The House on Mango Street, with a libretto she co-wrote, premiered at the Glimmerglass Festival in 2025. As of October 2026, her site says she lives in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, and is a citizen of both countries.
keyFacts: Born in Chicago to parents from Mexico; only daughter among seven children.
1984: The House on Mango Street.
1991: Woman Hollering Creek and Other Stories; 2002: Caramelo.
1995: MacArthur Fellowship; 2016: National Medal of Arts.

people.name: Lee Trevino
body: By age five, Lee Trevino was working in the onion and cotton fields of Garland, Texas. By eight he was collecting stray golf balls to sell, and later he worked as a caddie. He was raised by his mother, Juanita, and his grandfather, Joseph, a gravedigger. He was born December 1, 1939, in the Dallas area; the Texas Sports Hall of Fame says Rowlett and Encyclopedia.com says Dallas.

He left school before eighth grade. At 17 he lied about his age to join the U.S. Marines, served four years in Asia and played on the Third Marine Division's golf squad. He turned professional at 27. His first PGA Tour win was the 1968 U.S. Open. In 1971 he won the U.S. Open, the Canadian Open and the British Open within 20 days, becoming the first player to win all three in the same year. He won six major championships in all.

Trevino played on six U.S. Ryder Cup teams and captained the team in 1985. He won five Vardon Trophies for low scoring average and was inducted into the World Golf Hall of Fame in 1981. Other golfers nicknamed him "The Merry Mex" and "Super Mex."
keyFacts: Served four years in the U.S. Marines.
1968: U.S. Open, his first Tour victory.
1971: won the U.S., Canadian and British Opens in one season.
Six majors: U.S. Open 1968, 1971; British Open 1971, 1972; PGA 1974, 1984.
1981: World Golf Hall of Fame; 1985: U.S. Ryder Cup captain.

people.name: César Chávez
body: César Chávez was born March 31, 1927, on his family's farm near Yuma, Arizona. The Great Depression cost the family their land, and after eighth grade he joined them as a migrant farmworker in California. History.com reports that he served two years in the U.S. Navy from 1946, in a segregated unit.

He first organized with Fred Ross and the Community Service Organization, a Latino civil rights group. He left to focus on farmworkers and founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 Filipino farmworkers led by Larry Itliong struck in Delano, California, and the association joined them. The two unions merged into the United Farm Workers in 1966, with Chávez as president and Itliong as vice president. He died April 23, 1993, near Yuma. In 1994 President Bill Clinton awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The street at the center of St. Paul's West Side Cinco de Mayo parade has carried his name, but the West Side Community Organization is running a renaming vote on Nov. 3, 2026, among five names. Minnesota repealed Cesar Chavez Day in 2026, and the governor proclaimed Farmworkers Day.

In March 2026, the Associated Press and PBS NewsHour reported on a New York Times investigation that found he groomed and sexually abused young girls who worked in the movement. Dolores Huerta, co-founder of the union, said in a statement that he had sexually abused her, that she had kept silent for 60 years out of concern for the movement, and that the movement is larger than any one person. These are allegations reported by journalists, not court findings. PBS reported that some celebrations honoring him were canceled.
keyFacts: Born near Yuma, Arizona; migrant farmworker after eighth grade.
1962: founded the National Farm Workers Association.
1965: joined the Delano grape strike begun by Filipino workers.
1966: United Farm Workers formed.
2026: the abuse allegations described above became public.

people.name: Selena Quintanilla
body: In 1987, a teenage singer from South Texas won two of the top honors at the Tejano Music Awards: Best Female Vocalist and Performer of the Year. Selena Quintanilla had been the lead singer of her family's band since she was about ten.

Selena was born on April 16, 1971, in Lake Jackson, Texas. Her father, Abraham Quintanilla, built a family band around her, Selena y Los Dinos, which recorded seven albums from 1984 to 1988. She began formal Spanish lessons in 1990. After music executive José Behar saw her perform at the 1989 Tejano Music Awards, he signed her to EMI's Latin division. Her album Live! won the Grammy for Best Mexican-American Album at the 36th Grammy Awards in 1994, and Biography.com reports she was the first female Tejano artist to win it.

On March 31, 1995, Selena was shot and killed in Corpus Christi, Texas, by Yolanda Saldívar, the president of her fan club. She was 23. Saldívar was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. Dreaming of You, released that July, reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Biography.com calls it the first mostly Spanish-language album to top that chart, while Women in World History describes it as half English and half Spanish. In 1997 the film Selena brought her story to an even wider audience.

1989: signed to EMI Latin.
1994: Grammy for Best Mexican-American Album, for Live!
Killed March 31, 1995, at age 23.
1995: Dreaming of You reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

people.name: France A. Córdova
body: In 1969, Americans watched astronauts walk on the Moon. A young Stanford graduate and writer named France Córdova was one of them, and around the same time she saw a PBS documentary about neutron stars. Together they brought back the love of physics she had first felt in seventh grade.

Córdova was born on August 5, 1947, in Paris, where her father was working. He was a Mexican American importer and a West Point graduate. She grew up in La Puente, California, the oldest of 12 children. At her Catholic high school, girls were discouraged from studying science, and she was one of only five girls allowed into a junior-year physics class. At Stanford she studied English and did fieldwork in Mexico among the Zapotec people.

After working as a writer, including at the Los Angeles Times, she earned a Ph.D. from Caltech in 1979. At Los Alamos National Laboratory she researched radiation from white dwarfs and pulsars, and from 1989 to 1993 she led Penn State's Department of Astronomy and Astrophysics.

From 1993 to 1996 she was NASA's chief scientist, the first woman and the youngest person to hold the job. She then became vice chancellor for research at UC Santa Barbara, chancellor of UC Riverside starting in 2002, and president of Purdue University from 2007 to 2012. On March 31, 2014, she became the 14th director of the National Science Foundation, and she completed her six-year term on March 31, 2020. In 2019 she was inducted into the California Hall of Fame.

people.name: Hilda Solis
body: Hilda Solis was born in Los Angeles on October 20, 1957, the third of seven children. Her father came from Mexico and her mother from Nicaragua; they met in a citizenship class. Both worked in factories and joined unions. Her father was a Teamsters shop steward at a battery recycling plant, and his experience with lead poisoning on the job shaped her early awareness of labor and environmental issues. Her mother spent 20 years on the night shift of a Mattel assembly line. Their daughter would become U.S. Secretary of Labor.

Solis grew up in La Puente, California. She was the first in her family to go to college, entering Cal Poly Pomona through its Educational Opportunity Program and earning a political science degree in 1979, then a master's in public administration from the University of Southern California in 1981. Early on she worked in the Carter White House Office of Hispanic Affairs and at the Office of Management and Budget.

Her first elected office was on the Rio Hondo Community College board in 1985. In 1994 she became the first Latina elected to the California State Senate, where she wrote a 1999 environmental justice law, the first of its kind in the nation to become law. In 2000 she became the first woman to receive the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award.

From 2001 to 2009 she represented California's 32nd District in Congress. Confirmed as Secretary of Labor on February 24, 2009, she served until January 2013 and was the first Latina to lead a federal executive department. She joined the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors in December 2014. As of October 2026, she is First District Supervisor, and the county's site calls her board chair.

people.name: Maria Hinojosa
body: In 2022, a seven-part podcast called Suave won the Pulitzer Prize for Audio Reporting. It looks at juvenile life sentences through one man's story. The journalist behind it, Maria Hinojosa, had long been bringing Latino stories into American newsrooms.

Hinojosa was born in Mexico City in 1961, raised in Chicago, and studied at Barnard College in New York. By the Murrow Symposium's account, she was the first Latina in many of the newsrooms where she worked. She has reported for NPR, PBS, CBS, CNN and WNBC.

Her best-known work is Latino USA, which she anchors and executive-produces. It has won a Peabody Award and calls itself the longest-running Latino news and cultural program on public radio. In 2010 she founded the Futuro Media Group, an independent nonprofit newsroom in Harlem, which produces Latino USA and Suave.

Her honors include four Emmys, the John Chancellor Award, two Robert F. Kennedy Journalism Awards and the 2024 Edward R. Murrow Lifetime Achievement Award. As of October 2026, Barnard lists her as Distinguished Journalist-in-Residence.

people.name: Richard E. Cavazos
body: In June 1953, during the Korean War, a young lieutenant from South Texas led a raid on an entrenched enemy position. He was wounded, but he kept going back out to bring in fallen and injured soldiers. For that he received the Distinguished Service Cross. On January 3, 2025, more than seven years after his death, President Joe Biden awarded him the Medal of Honor for those actions. His name was Richard E. Cavazos, and he went on to become the Army's first Hispanic four-star general.

Cavazos was born on January 31, 1929, in Kingsville, Texas. He graduated from Texas Technological College in 1951 with a geology degree and was commissioned that year. In Korea he served with the 65th Infantry Regiment and earned a Silver Star in February 1953.

In 1967 he went to Vietnam as a lieutenant colonel commanding the 1st Battalion, 18th Infantry. Near Loc Ninh he directed a counterattack under fire and earned a second Distinguished Service Cross. In 1976 he became the first Hispanic brigadier general, and in 1982 the first Hispanic four-star general. He went on to command U.S. Army Forces Command and retired in 1984 after 33 years of service.

Cavazos died in San Antonio on October 29, 2017, at age 88, from complications of Alzheimer's disease, and was buried at Fort Sam Houston National Cemetery. On May 9, 2023, Fort Hood in Texas was renamed Fort Cavazos in his honor. In 2025 the post was renamed Fort Hood again, this time for Col. Robert B. Hood, a World War I officer.
keyFacts: Born in Kingsville, Texas; commissioned 1951.
Distinguished Service Cross, Korea (1953) and Vietnam (1967).
1976: first Hispanic brigadier general; 1982: first Hispanic four-star general.
January 3, 2025: Medal of Honor, for his actions in Korea.
Fort Hood was named Fort Cavazos from 2023 until 2025.

people.name: María Fernanda Castro Maya
body: María Fernanda Castro Maya is a Mexican woman with an intellectual disability and a self-advocate with CONFE. She began self-advocacy training in 2018 and joined groups of women with intellectual disabilities. In 2020 Inclusion International named her a regional representative for Empower Us, its self-advocacy group.

That year she led an online consultation on political participation and moderated a workshop at the Global Self-Advocacy Summit. In 2021 she moderated a consultation on deinstitutionalization and spoke at a United Nations side event on political rights. Human Rights Watch gave her age as 29 in 2022. She lives in Mexico and is not Mexican American.

Empower Us regional representative, Inclusion International, from 2020.

people.name: Luis Alfonso García
body: Luis Alfonso García was born at Hospital de la Raza in Mexico City and was told he had an intellectual disability at about age 8. He attends the Sembradores Special Education Center, where he learned about his rights, and is supported by CONFE. He took self-advocacy courses in 2018 and 2021, joined a 2021 COVID-19 focus group, and completed a regional leadership course for young people with disabilities in Latin America and the Caribbean.

At Sembradores he has worked as a therapeutic companion for classmates with disabilities. He told Human Rights Watch, which gave his age as 24 in 2022, that he wants to take part in Mexico's political life to exercise his own rights and defend those of other disabled people. He lives in Mexico and is not Mexican American.
keyFacts: Born in Mexico City; told of his diagnosis at about age 8.

institutions.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe Church
aliases: Our Lady of Guadalupe Diocesan Shrine
Our Lady of Guadalupe Catholic Church
Our Lady of Guadalupe Catholic Church, St. Paul
body: In 1931, a guild of Catholic women rented space in a grocery store at 123 South Wabasha on St. Paul's West Side and started a "Mexican Mission." Mexican families living on the river flats below the bluffs had come north to work, and the mission gave them a place to worship in Spanish. The archdiocese calls it the first Spanish-speaking church in Minnesota.

The mission later moved into a former pool hall, and the community eventually bought the whole building. It was incorporated as a parish in 1939. Its later site at 286 East Fairfield flooded often. With the clearance of the West Side Flats, the parish bought land farther south and east and completed a new church at 401 Concord in 1961.

By the archdiocese's account, its pastors and women religious ran educational, social and legal assistance programs. Sister Mary Giovanni Gourhan of the School Sisters of Notre Dame, known as "Sister G," arrived in 1963, started a summer program in 1964 and in 1967 founded the Guadalupe Alternative Program, now called GAP. MNopedia names it the Guadalupe Area Plan, proposed in 1966 and operating by 1967. Since the 1970s, other Latino communities have joined the parish. It has been named a diocesan shrine.
keyFacts: 1931: founded as a Mexican Mission in a rented West Side storefront.
1939: incorporated as a parish.
1961: new church completed at 401 Concord.
1966 to 1967: The Guadalupe Area Plan (now GAP) was proposed in 1966 and operating by 1967, according to MNopedia; Sister Giovanni founded the Guadalupe Alternative Program.

institutions.name: Centro Tyrone Guzman
body: Centro began in 1974 in a living room. By its own history, it grew out of the Chicano Movement, as activists in Minneapolis met to talk about police brutality, high dropout rates and barriers to schooling and health care. MNopedia contrasts it with earlier Latino groups in the Twin Cities, which were usually tied to the Catholic Church: Centro Cultural Chicano was organized and run by Chicanos themselves.

Gloria Gallegos, Manuel P. Guzman and Donn J. Vargas incorporated Centro on February 5, 1974. MNopedia lists its founders as Irene Gomez-Bethke, Eulalia "Lolly" Reyes de Smith, Alma Samuel, Maria Gomez, Ramona Arreguin de Rosales and Marcela L. Trujillo; Centro's own pages say it was founded by artists, scholars, poets and students. From the living room it moved to a small office on Franklin Avenue, and a 1976 McKnight Foundation grant let it lease its first building, at 1800 Olson Highway.

Centro published the newspaper Visiones de la Raza and produced the radio program La Voz del Pueblo. In 1996, Tyrone Guzman became executive director, moved Centro to its current home and refocused it on education across generations. During his 13 years, Centro founded the bilingual preschool Siembra and started the Raíces youth program. He died in 2009, and in 2014 the organization took his name.

As of October 2026, its programs include Siembra Montessori, Follow Along developmental screening, Raíces, Wise Elders, caregiver respite and Manos Montessori, and it marks more than 50 years of service.
keyFacts: February 5, 1974: incorporated as Centro Cultural Chicano.
1996–2009: Tyrone Guzman's tenure as executive director.
2014: renamed Centro Tyrone Guzman.
Offers caregiver respite and early developmental screening.

institutions.name: National Museum of Mexican Art
body: In 1982, Chicago educator Carlos Tortolero and a group of fellow educators founded the Mexican Fine Arts Center Museum. The museum opened in 1987. In 2001 it moved into a 48,000-square-foot building in Pilsen, and in 2006 it took the name National Museum of Mexican Art.

The museum's history page says its collection holds more than 22,000 works, from ancient Mexico to the present, and that it was the first Latino museum accredited by the American Alliance of Museums. It reports reaching more than 150,000 visitors a year, including 52,000 K–12 students, and its website labels admission "Always Free."
keyFacts: 1982: founded by Carlos Tortolero and fellow educators.
1987: opened to the public.
2006: renamed the National Museum of Mexican Art.
First Latino museum accredited by the American Alliance of Museums, by its own account.

institutions.name: CONFE
aliases: Confederación Mexicana de Organizaciones en favor de la Persona con Discapacidad Intelectual
body: In 1975, two families and a teacher joined efforts to offer training and promote the rights of people with intellectual disabilities. In 1978, parents and professionals founded CONFE in Mexico City, on the initiative of Juan Vidal Graell (1934–2014). By its own history, it moved in 1995 to its current site in Cuajimalpa, on land donated by Vidal, and by 2008 it was a network of 114 associations. It now describes itself as a network of families and 115 organizations across Mexico.

Its services include early intervention, support for inclusive education and a job inclusion agency, which it says has 456 people working and more than 70 partner employers. It also works on rights and public policy and supports self-advocates, including María Fernanda Castro Maya and Luis Alfonso García.
keyFacts: 1978: founded by parents and professionals in Mexico City.
Network of families and 115 organizations, by its own account.
Supports self-advocates (autogestores).

institutions.name: Fiesta Educativa
institutions.location: Lincoln Heights, Los Angeles, California, with other California offices
body: Fiesta Educativa was founded in 1978 by the Eastern Los Angeles Regional Center and is now independent. Irene Martinez, a long-time Spanish teacher hired there as a counselor, organized a workshop for Latino families that helped lead to its creation. She was one of its original board members and has been executive director since 1998.

It works with Latino families of children, youth and adults with disabilities so that they know their rights and services. It runs statewide family conferences, an autism education program for parents and Fiestas Familiares, Spanish-language home gatherings about special education and Regional Center services. It is not in Minnesota, and its site says "Latino," not "Mexican."
keyFacts: Founded in 1978; offices in Los Angeles, Orange County, Riverside, San Bernardino and San Jose.
Works with Latino clients at 10 of California's 21 Regional Centers, by its own account.
Runs Spanish-language home gatherings for parents.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Mexican heritage includes people born in Minnesota over several generations, recent immigrants, mixed-status families, and people with Indigenous Mexican roots who may speak languages other than Spanish. No Minnesota study of Mexican-heritage families alone and disability was found, but Minnesota evidence on Latino and Hispanic families exists: a 2014 Department of Health study with 17 Latino parents, 2021 reports for the Department of Human Services on service use, and University of Minnesota autism tracking with 2022 data. The two main studies below are small, from Southern California, and about parents of autistic children, so they say little about adults or about physical, sensory or Deaf experience.
questions: What words do you or your family use for your condition, or your child's? Which words do you want me to use?
Who gave you a label or a diagnosis? Has it helped, or has it got in the way?
What do you want a label or an assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Which language do you want to use with me, and which interpreter would you like? Is it Spanish, an Indigenous language, or something else?
Who else helps you make decisions or give care, including relatives in Mexico? Who should be part of this, and who should not?
Is there anything you want to know about who sees your information, and why, before we go further?
What gets in the way of appointments for you, such as work hours, transportation, cost or worry about going somewhere?
Are faith, a parish or other healers part of your support? Would you like any of them connected to this?
Who first noticed the concern, and what did you think about it then?
Who has helped you find your way through services so far, such as another parent, a teacher or an organization?

context.heading: What one study of parents said about autism
body: In focus groups in Southern California with 25 immigrant parents of autistic children, the words most linked to autism were amor (love), buscar ayuda (looking for help) and niño especial (special child). Parents gave mostly biomedical causes: vaccines, genetics, or genetics plus environment. Some talked about family history, including the idea that a trait skipped a generation (Cohen and Miguel, 2018). This sample of 25 describes those parents only.

Stigma was a common theme. Parents described negative judgments of their child's behavior and of their parenting, including at large family gatherings, and many responded by educating relatives and neighbors. The authors describe that as a strength.

sources.label: Cohen and Miguel, Amor and Social Stigma, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2018)

context.heading: Faith
body: A U.S. study of 250 parents of Mexican and Puerto Rican origin, whose young children had developmental delays, found that most called themselves religious and saw both church and personal faith as supportive, with faith giving more support. Parents also used religious frameworks to make sense of their child's disability (Skinner and colleagues, 2001).

Cohen and Miguel summarize earlier work in which some Latino parents saw a disabled child as a punishment from God, others as a gift, and others as a test. That summary is older, secondhand and not specific to Mexican-heritage families. Ask, and treat faith as a possible partner only if the person wants that.

sources.label: Skinner, Correa, Skinner and Bailey, American Journal on Mental Retardation (2001), abstract
Cohen and Miguel, Amor and Social Stigma, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2018)

context.heading: Family, who notices, and who decides
body: In interviews with six undocumented Mexican mothers of autistic children in Southern California, someone other than the mother first raised the concern in five of six cases: an older sibling, a teacher or school staff. Mothers led the search for services, and in one family the diagnosis moved forward after the father accepted the concern. One mother's children lived in Mexico for about 15 years while she worked in the U.S. Do not assume who decides, or that relatives are nearby (Luelmo and colleagues, 2020).

The same authors cite earlier research in which some Mexican-heritage mothers did not expect speech before age 3, and they used familismo, a family-centered orientation, to build trust. Cohen and Miguel suggest that an expectation of respeto may bear on how some parents respond to certain autism therapies. Neither is a prediction about a family. Hear the person directly, even if a relative speaks first.

sources.label: Luelmo, Sandoval and Kasari, International Journal of Developmental Disabilities (2020, in print 2022)
Cohen and Miguel, Amor and Social Stigma, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2018)

context.heading: Fear of enforcement, documents and language
body: In the same study of six mothers, fear of deportation delayed help. One mother feared the regional center was a gancho, a trap, and put off seeking a diagnosis for years. Some held back answers during evaluations. Without a Social Security number, some families could not get services such as respite care. Language was a barrier for all six, and five of the six children were diagnosed at age 4 or older. Those mothers lived under California's system, not Minnesota's.

What helped was community organizations, parent support groups, other parents who explained IEPs, and a speech therapist who guided one family. For staff: say plainly what is shared and with whom. Explain which services do not depend on a Social Security number only after you confirm the program rules. Do not read a missed appointment as lack of interest, and do not use children as interpreters.

sources.label: Luelmo, Sandoval and Kasari, International Journal of Developmental Disabilities (2020, in print 2022)

context.heading: Words
body: Parents in these two studies used niño especial, amor, buscar ayuda, confianza (trust), gancho and la migra (immigration enforcement). Mexican disability organizations use persona con discapacidad and discapacidad intelectual, and autogestores for self-advocates. No source was found that lists stigmatizing Spanish terms specific to Mexican communities, so none are offered here. Check that written Spanish is plain, and that it is understood without relying on the paper alone.

sources.label: Cohen and Miguel, Amor and Social Stigma, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2018)
Luelmo, Sandoval and Kasari, International Journal of Developmental Disabilities (2020, in print 2022)
CONFE, Historia
Human Rights Watch, People with Intellectual Disabilities Should Have Representation (2022)

context.heading: What could not be found
body: This review found no research on Minnesota's Mexican-heritage families alone and disability (Minnesota studies of Latino and Hispanic families are named in the introduction), none on adults, and none on physical, sensory or Deaf disability in this population. The studies reviewed do not examine curanderismo or other traditional healing, so no claim is made about it. No Minnesota Mexican American disabled leader with a public record to profile could be found either, so the two people on this page are self-advocates in Mexico. Several relevant studies of Mexican American mothers could not be obtained.

organizations.intro: Mexican Minnesotans have roots on St. Paul's West Side going back more than a century, and Sahan Journal describes the West Side as the heart of the city's Mexican community. Minnesota Compass counts 231,993 people in its Mexican cultural community, out of 5,739,445 Minnesotans, the largest of the Latino-origin groups it lists. It uses the American Community Survey for 2020–2024, with a margin of error of about 5,615; the count rests on self-reported race, ancestry and birthplace, including parents', and has survey error. Sahan Journal cited about 180,000 Latino residents across the Twin Cities metro in 2020, a figure for all Latino groups. The state's 2026 agency summary for the Latino Affairs Council reports about 381,000 Latino Minnesotans statewide. MPR News reported in April 2026 that a surge of federal agents (called Operation Metro Surge in other reporting) had made for a very long winter on the West Side, and that neighbors watched local businesses and delivered food. Other reporting describes the June 14, 2026 closing of Colonial Market on Lake Street and an 85 percent drop in January revenue at Mercado Central. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.
